title: Super reforms to ban cold calls
full_text:
Cold calling in super will be banned and the trustee-for-hire model effectively killed off as the federal government looks to prevent another Shield or First Guardian scandal.
On Wednesday Financial Services Minister Daniel Mulino will reveal details of a long-awaited package of consumer protection and financial advice reforms, with a sweetener built in for big super.
As revealed exclusively by The Australian this month, a crackdown on cold calling in super is top of Dr Mulino’s list in the wake of the $1bn Shield and First Guardian investment scandal that cost 11,000 Australians their super savings.
Unlicensed real-time communication about super will no longer be allowed and the government will tighten the anti-hawking loophole that allows advisers to cold call prospective clients. Under the reforms, advisers will be allowed to make unsolicited calls only to existing clients.
“These reforms are designed to disrupt some of the most damaging business models operating in the system today,” Dr Mulino will say at the National Press Club on Wednesday.
“They target the point at which consumers are first exposed to harm and reduce the ability of bad actors to gain access to consumers in the first place. We will make the financial system safer by strengthening protections across the superannuation, advice and investment ecosystem.” Dr Mulino also is expected to unveil sweeping changes for platforms and trustees designed to enhance consumer protections in the event of another financial scandal and make the trustee-for-hire model commercially unviable.
Super trustees will be required to hold enough capital to be able to compensate investors in the event of significant losses. This essentially will kill off the trustee-for-hire model by proxy, since it would require the outsourced trustee to take on substantial financial risk.
The move against outsourced trustees comes after Equity Trustees and Diversa, both classed as trustees for hire, declined to compensate investors caught up in the Shield and First Guardian mess. Both are in court fighting allegations brought by the corporate regulator that they failed to do due diligence on the now collapsed funds.
In contrast, Macquarie and Netwealth, both operating in-house super trustee models, compensated affected investors to the tune of $421m. Equity Trustees has since put its super trustee business up for sale The government also is planning on bringing in mandatory education requirements for anyone wanting to establish a self-managed super fund, and the Australian Taxation Office and the Australian Securities & Investments Commission will have greater information-sharing powers to detect unusual patterns in super switching.
The ATO also will be able to pause rollovers from APRA-regulated funds to SMSFs if fraud is detected. Dr Mulino is also expected to address advice reforms that have been on the backburner for more than a year.
